Tech Stack - Personal Assistant

The personal assistant is built using FastAPI for the async backend, 
ChromaDB for local vector storage, sentence-transformers for embeddings, 
and Gemini 2.0 Flash as the LLM for response generation. Anshu chose 
ChromaDB over cloud vector databases because the data is small and 
personal, making a local solution simpler and free. She chose not to use 
LangGraph for this project unlike ResumeIQ, because the pipeline is 
linear with no complex state management or conditional routing â€” adding 
LangGraph would have been over-engineering. This decision demonstrates 
her ability to choose the right tool for the right problem rather than 
using the same stack for everything. Session memory is handled using a 
simple in-memory dictionary rather than a database, keeping the 
architecture lightweight for a portfolio use case.

recommendations. It makes 3 LLM calls per analysis 
and is live at https://agentic-resume-analyzer.netlify.app/

pipeline with ChromaDB, sentence transformers,

anything about Anshu's background or paste a job

against her resume.

What makes these two projects compelling together 
is that they are integrated â€” the personal assistant 
calls ResumeIQ as a live tool, making two of Anshu's 
projects work together as one system. This 
demonstrates her ability to design, build, and 
connect end-to-end AI systems from scratch.

Project - Personal Assistant (Overview)

Anshu built an AI-powered personal assistant that acts as a talking 
portfolio for recruiters and hiring managers. The assistant can answer 
questions about Anshu's skills, projects, education, and experience. It 
is deployed as a full stack web application with a FastAPI backend and a 
clean dark-themed frontend. Recruiters can either type questions freely 
or use quick-access buttons for common topics like skills, education, and 
projects.

Project - ResumeIQ (Architecture and Workflow)

ResumeIQ is built as a stateful LangGraph pipeline with 4 nodes: extract, 
agent, tools, and analyze. When a user uploads their resume and a job 
description, the system first uses PyMuPDF to extract raw text from the PDF. 
The extract node then uses a llama-3.1-8b-instant model to parse this text 
into a structured JSON containing skills, experience, projects, and required 
and preferred skills from the JD. This structured data is stored in the 
LangGraph state and passed forward through the pipeline.

The agent node receives this structured data and makes an LLM call using the 
20b parameter model to decide which tools to invoke based on the identified 
skill gaps. The ATS keyword checker is hardcoded to always run, while the 
agent autonomously chooses whether to call the Adzuna job market API and the 
YouTube Data API based on what gaps it finds in the candidate's profile.

The tools node executes the decided tools and updates the state with their 
results. Finally the analyze node receives the full state â€” resume data, JD 
data, and all tool results â€” and makes a third LLM call using the 20b model 
with a structured prompt to generate a comprehensive analysis. The graph 
structure is linear: extract â†’ agent â†’ tools â†’ analyze â†’ END. Chat 
functionality is handled outside the graph, called directly from the REST API 
endpoint.

In total ResumeIQ makes 3 LLM calls per full analysis: one in the extract 
node using the 8b model, one in the agent node, and one in the analyze node 
both using the 20b model.

Project - ResumeIQ (Future Scope)

Anshu has planned several meaningful extensions for ResumeIQ. A resume 
rewrite tool that automatically rewrites the candidate's resume to better 
match JD keywords and improve the ATS score is high on the list. An interview 
mode is also planned where the system will conduct a mock interview based on 
the resume and JD requirements, asking role-relevant questions and evaluating 
answers. A multi-resume comparison feature is also being considered, allowing 
candidates to compare two versions of their resume side by side against the 
same JD.

Project - ResumeIQ (Token Management and Chat)

One of the hardest engineering challenges Anshu solved in ResumeIQ was 
managing token usage wisely across the pipeline given the constraints of free 
tier LLM APIs. With a resume, job description, and tool results all being fed 
into prompts simultaneously, token usage can spike quickly. Anshu addressed 
this by using a smaller 8b model for the extraction node where structured 
output matters more than reasoning depth, and reserving the 20b model only 
for the agent and analysis nodes where quality is critical. This dual model 
architecture effectively doubled the token budget while maintaining output 
quality.

For chat memory Anshu implemented a custom history compression function that 
keeps the first 2 messages for context and the last 10 messages for 
continuity, discarding the middle of long conversations. This keeps the chat 
context window lean without losing important context. Instead of sending the 
full resume to every chat turn, only the extracted skills, experience, 
projects, and missing skills are sent â€” significantly reducing per-turn token 
consumption. Anshu is actively continuing to improve token efficiency in the 
project.

Project - ResumeIQ (Tool Orchestration)

ResumeIQ orchestrates 3 tools. The ATS keyword checker always runs as 
described above. The Adzuna job market API is called when the agent identifies 
skill gaps â€” it returns the number of active job listings for a skill and 
average salary data, giving the candidate a real sense of how in-demand their 
missing skills are in the current market. The YouTube Data API is called to 
find relevant learning resources for the missing skills, so the candidate gets 
actionable course recommendations directly in the analysis. The agent node 
uses an LLM call to autonomously decide which of the latter two tools to 
invoke based on the candidate's specific skill gaps.

Experience

Anshu completed a Web Development internship at Scoutbizz International 
from June 2025 to August 2025. During this internship she worked on 
production-level web applications and client websites. She customized Shopify 
storefronts using HTML, CSS, and Liquid templates, and collaborated with 
designers and developers to improve website performance and UI quality.

linear with no complex state management or conditional routing â€” adding

using the same stack for everything. Session memory is handled using a 
simple in-memory dictionary rather than a database, keeping the

portfolio for recruiters and hiring managers. The assistant can answer

projects.

keyword analysis, job market data from Adzuna, and course recommendations 
from YouTube â€” and returns a detailed analysis. The personal assistant then 
formats this analysis into a clean response. This makes the assistant not 
just a static Q&A system but a live demonstration of Anshu's agentic AI 
work, where two of her projects work together as an integrated system.

Tool Orchestration, and RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation). She has 
hands-on experience building Agentic AI systems and LLM-based pipelines.

used the Groq API for fast LLM inference, and has practical experience with 
Prompt Engineering and Tool Orchestration. She is familiar with RAG pipelines 
and is actively deepening her knowledge in this area through her personal 
assistant project.

Project Challenges - Personal Assistant

Building the personal assistant came with several 
interesting challenges. The first was deciding how 
to write and structure the personal data so it 
could be chunked properly for accurate retrieval. 
Anshu learned that natural conversational language 
retrieves far better than bullet point lists â€” so 
instead of writing her information like a resume, 
she wrote it as answers to questions a recruiter 
might ask. The second challenge was a RAG retrieval 
domination problem â€” when querying for all projects, 
ChromaDB was only returning ResumeIQ chunks because 
ResumeIQ had 5 chunks versus one chunk for other 
projects, crowding out smaller topics in semantic 
search. She fixed this by running two separate 
targeted queries per topic and combining the results, 
learning that data distribution in a vector database 
directly affects retrieval quality.  
These challenges taught Anshu that in AI systems, 
data quality and system design matter as much as 
model choice.

Project - ResumeIQ (Architecture and Workflow)

ResumeIQ is built as a stateful LangGraph pipeline with 4 nodes: extract, 
agent, tools, and analyze. When a user uploads their resume and a job 
description, the system first uses PyMuPDF to extract raw text from the PDF. 
The extract node then uses a llama-3.1-8b-instant model to parse this text 
into a structured JSON containing skills, experience, projects, and required 
and preferred skills from the JD. This structured data is stored in the 
LangGraph state and passed forward through the pipeline.

The agent node receives this structured data and makes an LLM call using the 
20b parameter model to decide which tools to invoke based on the identified 
skill gaps. The ATS keyword checker is hardcoded to always run, while the 
agent autonomously chooses whether to call the Adzuna job market API and the 
YouTube Data API based on what gaps it finds in the candidate's profile.

The tools node executes the decided tools and updates the state with their 
results. Finally the analyze node receives the full state â€” resume data, JD 
data, and all tool results â€” and makes a third LLM call using the 20b model 
with a structured prompt to generate a comprehensive analysis. The graph 
structure is linear: extract â†’ agent â†’ tools â†’ analyze â†’ END. Chat 
functionality is handled outside the graph, called directly from the REST API 
endpoint.

In total ResumeIQ makes 3 LLM calls per full analysis: one in the extract 
node using the 8b model, one in the agent node, and one in the analyze node 
both using the 20b model.

This section describes Anshu's personal journey and motivation 
for choosing AI as a career path.
Anshu chose AI because she finds it genuinely fascinating 
how artificial intelligence is transforming every industry 
and making people's lives easier in meaningful ways. Her 
journey started with Data Science, then deepened into 
Machine Learning, and eventually led her to Agentic AI 
systems. What excites her most is how AI can solve real 
world problems, automate complex tasks, and reduce human 
effort. Seeing how ChatGPT works, how image classification 
and object detection function, and how AI assists in 
complex medical surgeries â€” all of this motivated her to 
build in this space. She is driven by the belief that AI 
can be used to create tools that genuinely help people.

Goals - Roles Anshu is Looking For

Anshu is actively looking for entry level roles that 
combine backend engineering with AI. She is specifically 
interested in positions where she can build and deploy 
AI powered systems, work on LLM pipelines, agentic 
workflows, or RAG based applications. She is comfortable 
working across the full backend stack and enjoys 
integrating AI into production systems. She is open to 
both startups and larger companies and is particularly 
interested in teams building practical AI products. She 
is based in Pune, India and open to both remote and 
on-site opportunities.

Projects Overview

Anshu has built two end-to-end AI projects that 
work together as an integrated portfolio system.

Her first project, ResumeIQ, is a fully deployed 
agentic resume analyzer built using LangGraph with 
a 5 node pipeline. It analyzes a candidate's resume 
against a job description using ATS keyword matching, 
Adzuna job market data, and YouTube course 
recommendations. It makes 3 LLM calls per analysis 
and is live at https://agentic-resume-analyzer.netlify.app/

Her second project is this Personal Assistant â€” an 
AI powered talking portfolio built using a RAG 
pipeline with ChromaDB, sentence transformers, 
Gemini 3.5 Flash, and FastAPI. Recruiters can ask 
anything about Anshu's background or paste a job 
description to get a live ResumeIQ analysis run 
against her resume.

What makes these two projects compelling together 
is that they are integrated â€” the personal assistant 
calls ResumeIQ as a live tool, making two of Anshu's 
projects work together as one system. This 
demonstrates her ability to design, build, and 
connect end-to-end AI systems from scratch.

Introduction

Anshu is a Computer Science graduate from Truba Institute of Engineering 
and Information Technology, Bhopal, currently based in Pune, India. She is 
looking for entry-level opportunities in the AI and Machine Learning field. 
She is a fresher with hands-on experience building real-world AI 
systems, particularly in agentic AI, LLM pipelines, and RAG-based 
applications. She is passionate about building practical AI tools that solve 
real problems and is actively seeking roles where she can contribute to AI 
product development or research.

Project - Personal Assistant (Overview)

Anshu built an AI-powered personal assistant that acts as a talking 
portfolio for recruiters and hiring managers. The assistant can answer 
questions about Anshu's skills, projects, education, and experience. It 
is deployed as a full stack web application with a FastAPI backend and a 
clean dark-themed frontend. Recruiters can either type questions freely 
or use quick-access buttons for common topics like skills, education, and 
projects.

Project - Personal Assistant (ResumeIQ Integration)

The personal assistant integrates Anshu's ResumeIQ project as a live tool. 
Recruiters can paste a job description directly into the assistant and it 
will automatically call the ResumeIQ backend API with Anshu's resume and 
the provided JD. ResumeIQ runs its full agentic LangGraph pipeline â€” ATS 
keyword analysis, job market data from Adzuna, and course recommendations 
from YouTube â€” and returns a detailed analysis. The personal assistant then 
formats this analysis into a clean response. This makes the assistant not 
just a static Q&A system but a live demonstration of Anshu's agentic AI 
work, where two of her projects work together as an integrated system.

Contact and Availability

Anshu is currently based in Pune, India and is originally from Vidisha, 
Madhya Pradesh. She is actively looking for full-time opportunities in AI, 
Machine Learning, or backend engineering roles. She is open to both remote 
and on-site positions. Recruiters can reach her at anshusharma27165@gmail.com or 
connect with her on LinkedIn at https://www.linkedin.com/in/anshu-sharma-33b979268/. She is excited to 
bring her skills in agentic AI and LLM systems to a team working on 
impactful products.

Certifications

Anshu holds the Microsoft Certified Azure Fundamentals certification, 
demonstrating foundational knowledge of cloud concepts and Microsoft Azure 
services.

question: What was the hardest challenge in building ResumeIQ?
chunks:
Project Challenges - Personal Assistant

Building the personal assistant came with several 
interesting challenges. The first was deciding how 
to write and structure the personal data so it 
could be chunked properly for accurate retrieval. 
Anshu learned that natural conversational language 
retrieves far better than bullet point lists â€” so 
instead of writing her information like a resume, 
she wrote it as answers to questions a recruiter 
might ask. The second challenge was a RAG retrieval 
domination problem â€” when querying for all projects, 
ChromaDB was only returning ResumeIQ chunks because 
ResumeIQ had 5 chunks versus one chunk for other 
projects, crowding out smaller topics in semantic 
search. She fixed this by running two separate 
targeted queries per topic and combining the results, 
learning that data distribution in a vector database 
directly affects retrieval quality.  
These challenges taught Anshu that in AI systems, 
data quality and system design matter as much as 
model choice.

Project Challenges - Building ResumeIQ

The most technically challenging aspect of building ResumeIQ â€” 
and the hardest technical challenge Anshu faced was 
managing token limits and token usage across the pipeline 
given free tier LLM API constraints. With a resume, job 
description, and multiple tool results all being fed into 
prompts simultaneously, token usage spiked quickly and 
responses were getting cut off or degraded in quality. 
She solved this by splitting work across two models â€” 
using the smaller 8b model for the extraction node where 
structured output matters more than reasoning depth, and 
reserving the 70b model only for agent and analysis nodes 
where quality is critical. This dual model architecture 
effectively doubled the token budget while maintaining 
output quality. For chat memory she implemented a custom 
history compression function keeping the first 2 messages 
and last 10 messages, discarding the middle of long 
conversations to keep the context window lean. She also 
sends only extracted JSON fields to chat turns instead of 
the full resume text, significantly reducing per-turn 
token consumption. Anshu considers this the most valuable 
engineering lesson from ResumeIQ â€” that working within 
constraints forces smarter architectural decisions.

Project - ResumeIQ (Token Management and Chat)

One of the hardest engineering challenges Anshu solved in ResumeIQ was 
managing token usage wisely across the pipeline given the constraints of free 
tier LLM APIs. With a resume, job description, and tool results all being fed 
into prompts simultaneously, token usage can spike quickly. Anshu addressed 
this by using a smaller 8b model for the extraction node where structured 
output matters more than reasoning depth, and reserving the 20b model only 
for the agent and analysis nodes where quality is critical. This dual model 
architecture effectively doubled the token budget while maintaining output 
quality.

For chat memory Anshu implemented a custom history compression function that 
keeps the first 2 messages for context and the last 10 messages for 
continuity, discarding the middle of long conversations. This keeps the chat 
context window lean without losing important context. Instead of sending the 
full resume to every chat turn, only the extracted skills, experience, 
projects, and missing skills are sent â€” significantly reducing per-turn token 
consumption. Anshu is actively continuing to improve token efficiency in the 
project.

Project - ResumeIQ (Architecture and Workflow)

ResumeIQ is built as a stateful LangGraph pipeline with 4 nodes: extract, 
agent, tools, and analyze. When a user uploads their resume and a job 
description, the system first uses PyMuPDF to extract raw text from the PDF. 
The extract node then uses a llama-3.1-8b-instant model to parse this text 
into a structured JSON containing skills, experience, projects, and required 
and preferred skills from the JD. This structured data is stored in the 
LangGraph state and passed forward through the pipeline.

The agent node receives this structured data and makes an LLM call using the 
20b parameter model to decide which tools to invoke based on the identified 
skill gaps. The ATS keyword checker is hardcoded to always run, while the 
agent autonomously chooses whether to call the Adzuna job market API and the 
YouTube Data API based on what gaps it finds in the candidate's profile.

The tools node executes the decided tools and updates the state with their 
results. Finally the analyze node receives the full state â€” resume data, JD 
data, and all tool results â€” and makes a third LLM call using the 20b model 
with a structured prompt to generate a comprehensive analysis. The graph 
structure is linear: extract â†’ agent â†’ tools â†’ analyze â†’ END. Chat 
functionality is handled outside the graph, called directly from the REST API 
endpoint.

In total ResumeIQ makes 3 LLM calls per full analysis: one in the extract 
node using the 8b model, one in the agent node, and one in the analyze node 
both using the 20b model.

pipeline with ChromaDB, sentence transformers,

anything about Anshu's background or paste a job 
description to get a live ResumeIQ analysis run 
against her resume.

What makes these two projects compelling together 
is that they are integrated â€” the personal assistant 
calls ResumeIQ as a live tool, making two of Anshu's 
projects work together as one system. This 
demonstrates her ability to design, build, and 
connect end-to-end AI systems from scratch.

Project - ResumeIQ (Future Scope)

Anshu has planned several meaningful extensions for ResumeIQ. A resume 
rewrite tool that automatically rewrites the candidate's resume to better 
match JD keywords and improve the ATS score is high on the list. An interview 
mode is also planned where the system will conduct a mock interview based on 
the resume and JD requirements, asking role-relevant questions and evaluating 
answers. A multi-resume comparison feature is also being considered, allowing 
candidates to compare two versions of their resume side by side against the 
same JD.

Project - ResumeIQ (ATS Keyword Checker)

The ATS keyword checker is a custom Python function Anshu built from scratch. 
It computes a keyword match percentage between the resume and job description 
using set intersection â€” finding matched keywords as the intersection of JD 
words and resume words, and missing keywords as the difference. The match 
percentage is calculated as the number of matched keywords divided by total JD 
keywords multiplied by 100. It also checks resume formatting by verifying 
whether standard sections like skills, education, projects, and experience 
exist in the resume, and flags any missing sections as formatting issues. The 
function returns the match percentage, top matched and missing keywords, 
formatting issues, and an overall ATS pass or fail based on whether the match 
percentage is above 60 percent and there are no formatting issues.

Project - ResumeIQ (Tool Orchestration)

ResumeIQ orchestrates 3 tools. The ATS keyword checker always runs as 
described above. The Adzuna job market API is called when the agent identifies 
skill gaps â€” it returns the number of active job listings for a skill and 
average salary data, giving the candidate a real sense of how in-demand their 
missing skills are in the current market. The YouTube Data API is called to 
find relevant learning resources for the missing skills, so the candidate gets 
actionable course recommendations directly in the analysis. The agent node 
uses an LLM call to autonomously decide which of the latter two tools to 
invoke based on the candidate's specific skill gaps.

The most difficult engineering challenge Anshu faced while building **ResumeIQ** was **managing token limits and token usage across the entire pipeline** under the constraints of free‑tier LLM APIs.

  - Excessive tokens led to truncated responses and degraded output quality.  

- **How Anshu solved it:**

results. Finally the analyze node receives the full state â€” resume data, JD 
data, and all tool results â€” and makes a third LLM call using the 20b model 
with a structured prompt to generate a comprehensive analysis. The graph 
structure is linear: extract â†’ agent â†’ tools â†’ analyze â†’ END. Chat 
functionality is handled outside the graph, called directly from the REST API 
endpoint.

both using the 20b model.
